newsitem.title: UK: Herpes could cause Alzheimer's, scientists say.
newsitem.headline: Herpes could cause Alzheimer's, scientists say.

text.p: The herpes virus that causes cold sores may be teaming up with a genetic mutation to cause damage that leads to Alzheimer's disease, British researchers said on Friday.

Ruth Itzhaki and colleagues at the University of Manchester found that people with the variant of a gene known as apolipoprotein-E (APOE) who also had herpes infections of the brain were much more likely to have Alzheimer's.

Researchers have long suspected that herpes (HSV-1) might be involved in Alzheimer's. Almost everyone is infected with HSV-1, although not everyone gets cold sores and there is no indication that herpes infection of the brain is common.
Several other neurological disorders are known to be caused by viruses and herpes is found in the same areas of the brain that are affected in Alzheimer's, the researchers added.

Itzhaki's group analysed DNA from the brains of 90 people with and without Alzheimer's. They found 52.8 percent of Alzheimer's patients who had the herpes virus in their brains also had the APOE-epsilon 4 mutation.
Only 10 percent of Alzheimer's patients without the virus in their brains had the mutation, and only a very few of the non-Alzheimer's patients.

"These findings suggest that the combination of HSV-1 in the brain and carriage of an APOE-epsilon 4 (gene) is a strong risk factor for Alzheimer's disease, whereas either of these features alone does not increase the risk of Alzheimer's," they wrote in a report in the Lancet medical journal.
"The findings in people with cold sores support our hypothesis that APOE-epsilon 4 and HSV-1 together are damaging in the nervous system."
They said the involvement of herpes in Alzheimer's could explain why anti-inflammatory drugs can prevent or delay onset of Alzheimer's symptoms, because inflammation can reactivate herpes episodes.
Younger volunteers did not have herpes in their brains, which could indicate that as the immune system weakens with age, the virus can spread to the central nervous system.
Their findings could be used to look for new treatments for Alzheimer's, especially antivirals or anti-inflammatories.
"In addition, our data call into question the proposed use of HSV-1 as a vector for gene therapy." Gene therapy often involves using a virus to deliver altered DNA into a patient.
Alzheimer's, which causes dementia and disorientation, affects about 10 percent of people aged over 65 worldwide.
The herpes family of viruses causes cold sores, chicken pox, shingles and a variety of other diseases. Once a herpes virus infects someone it stays in the nerve cells forever.
